title: Project: unit conversion
goal: Build a converter with independent functions and separate computation and interface checks.

prerequisites.text: Declare functions and verify a numerical contract independently of input.

terms.title: Unit conversion
terms.definition: Restating the same quantity in different units.

sections.title: Why it matters
paragraphs: Hours and minutes measure time; kilograms and grams measure mass. A function owns its factor, while the printed unit belongs to the interface.
State each numerical contract first. Then let main validate input, dispatch to the right function and print the result.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Predict the results for 3 hours and 2 kilograms. Identify both factors and labels.

sections.title: Diagnostics
paragraphs: A correct value with the wrong unit can indicate a dispatch or output error. A direct call checks the formula.
Clang reports an undeclared function when a call misspells its name. Compare it with the declaration.

sections.title: Transfer to practice
paragraphs: Choice 1 converts minutes to seconds, and choice 2 converts kilometers to meters. At the maximum 30, 30 × 1000 = 30000 fits the minimum C17 int range.

If a direct conversion call returns the right number but the display labels it with the other unit, check branch selection and output formatting separately. With an unknown code, calculation should never start.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Build a converter with independent functions and separate computation and interface checks.

selfcheck.prompt: What should be checked if a kilometer input gives seconds 3000?
feedback: The value is already right for three kilometers.

selfcheck.prompt: How can the meter calculation, dispatch and rejection of an unknown unit be checked separately?
selfcheck.feedback: Call kilometers_to_meters(3) directly and check 3000. Then check code 2 with 3 km and its meters label. Code 3 must give invalid before any calculation.

static int meters(int kilometers) { return kilometers * 1000; }
int main(void) { return metre(3); }

practice.title: Time and distance converter
practice.task: The first line contains code 1 or 2 and the second a magnitude from 0 to 30. Code 1 converts minutes to seconds and code 2 kilometers to meters. Fix both functions. Print seconds or meters before the result, or invalid for rejected input. The supplied read_integer function checks the first two lines. A missing line, an invalid number or an out-of-range value gives invalid. The program ignores any later input.
practice.hint: Each function has its own factor. Try an ordinary case and the maximum of 30 km.
criteria: 1 and 2 give seconds 120; 2 and 3 give meters 3000.
Unknown code 3 and a missing magnitude are rejected.
Calculation functions do not read or print.
Two direct calls with empty input gave 120 3000. A separate run of the main program with code 3 gave invalid.

steps.action: Enter 2 and 3 on separate lines, then run the starter.
steps.why: Build a converter with independent functions and separate computation and interface checks.
steps.expected: The starter prints meters 3. Converting 3 km to meters should give meters 3000.

steps.action: Fix the formula in each function. In the working program, try 1 and 2, then 2 and 30.
steps.why: The change must satisfy the contract.
steps.expected: The working program prints seconds 120 and meters 30000 for those two runs.

steps.action: Save a copy of the entire corrected main.c in a separate text file. In the lesson editor, temporarily replace only the body of main. Call minutes_to_seconds(2) and kilometers_to_meters(3) from main, print the two results separated by a space and run with empty input.
steps.why: Two direct calls check the calculations independently of input parsing and unit dispatch.

steps.action: Restore the saved main.c in the lesson editor. Enter code 3 and magnitude 2 on separate lines, then run the working program.
steps.why: This checks rejection at the program interface.

exercises.title: Independent transfer
exercises.task: Create two direct calls before integration and check an unknown code through the main interface. Label what each test measures.
criteria: The two numerical results can be checked without stdin.
An invalid choice is rejected before calculation.

teaching.scene: A receiving station converts time and mass, then shows labels on its display. Separate the numbers returned by the functions from the lines assembled by the caller.

predict.prompt: main supplies 3 hours and 2 kilograms. What does each converter return, and where are the labels attached?
predict.answer: hours_to_minutes returns 3 × 60 = 180. kilograms_to_grams returns 2 × 1000 = 2000. main adds the labels, producing minutes 180 and grams 2000.

apply.prompt: Both branches of the new converter receive 0. Can the matching numbers confirm the choice of units and both multipliers? Name one extra observation for each property.
apply.answer: The zero results must have distinct labels: seconds 0 and meters 0. The numeric result does not test the multipliers. Give both branches a nonzero value such as 4 to check the calculation: expect seconds 240 and meters 4000.

practice.strategy: State each function’s input and output units. Test both formulas with direct calls in a local copy. In the working program, separately check dispatch and rejection of an unknown code.
practice.diagnosis: An output of meters 3 for three kilometers shows input and dispatch reached the meter branch. Check the multiplier in the distance conversion function.

syntax.explanation: A conversion function takes a number and returns the value in another unit. Dispatch and the printed unit remain the caller’s responsibility.
syntax.mistake: When a converter prints its own label, the numeric result is harder to test in isolation. Compare the returned value separately.
